This is the horizontal reading of a teaching usually taken vertically. It is not just individual faith that unlocks the power. It is reconciliation. When two people who were at odds — spouses, siblings, colleagues, community members — make actual peace, something is released that can move what looks immovable. This tracks with the whole Jesus Way. Where two or three gather in my name, I am there. Love your neighbor as yourself. First be reconciled to your brother, then bring your gift. The mechanism of the kingdom is relational. Isolated piety does not move mountains. Reconciled community does. Thomas 106 makes the same claim — when you make the two into one, you will become sons of Adam, and when you say mountain move, it will move. The message is consistent. Peace between people is the power source. That is not mysticism. That is how the kingdom actually operates.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Blessed are the solitary and elect, for you will find the kingdom. For you are from it, and to it you will return."
title: The Solitary Will Find It
pullquote: You came from the kingdom. You'll return to it. And the ones who become whole find it first.
core_message: The undivided self recognizes its origin in the kingdom and its return to it.
context:
Blessed are the solitary and elect, for you will find the kingdom. Solitary here does not mean lonely or antisocial. The Coptic word behind it, *monachos*, means single, unified, whole — the same root behind Thomas 22's making the two into one. The solitary are the ones who have integrated the divided self, who no longer live pulled between competing loyalties, who have become simple in the deep sense of the word.

And the reason they find the kingdom is given in the next line. You are from it, and to it you will return. The kingdom is your origin and your destination. You are not trying to earn entry into an unfamiliar country. You are trying to remember the place you came from. The mystical logic of Thomas keeps circling this. Thomas 50 will spell it out — we came from the light. Thomas 18 said find the beginning and you find the end. This is the same teaching in yet another key. The scattered self loses the way because it cannot hold still long enough to recognize where it actually is. The solitary — the integrated — recognizes home. And going home is what the whole path is for.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "If they say to you, 'Where did you come from?', say to them, 'We came from the light, the place where the light came into being on its own accord and established itself and became manifest through their image.' If they say to you, 'Is it you?', say, 'We are its children, we are the elect of the living father.' If they ask you, 'What is the sign of your father in you?', say to them, 'It is movement and repose.'"
title: Children of the Light
pullquote: Where did you come from? The light. Who are you? Its children. What is the sign? Movement and repose.
core_message: Your true identity is child of the light — and its signature in you is both action and rest.
context:
This is a catechism of the awakened. When the world challenges you, here is what to say. Where did you come from? From the light, the place where the light came into being on its own accord, established itself, and became manifest through their image. Notice the language — self-arising light. Not created light. The source. And that source made itself visible in image — the *imago dei* of Genesis, the divine likeness stamped on humanity.

Is it you? We are its children, the elect of the living Father. Not adopted strangers. Actual children. Sharing the nature of what we came from. And the sign, the mark, the evidence of the Father's presence in you? Movement and repose. Two words held in balance. Action and stillness. Engagement and contemplation. The mystical rhythm of the awakened life — able to move powerfully into the world in service of love, and able to rest deeply in the Father when the movement is done. Neither restless activism nor detached withdrawal. Both at once. Jesus himself modeled this — teaching all day, then withdrawing to pray. Feeding the crowds, then getting into a boat alone. Movement and repose. That is what a child of the light looks like in the world.

jesus_words: His disciples said to him, "When will the repose of the dead come about, and when will the new world come?" He said to them, "What you look forward to has already come, but you do not recognize it."
title: It Has Already Come
pullquote: You keep looking forward to the new world. It's already here. You just aren't recognizing it.
core_message: What most people wait for as future has already arrived — the failure is recognition, not timing.
context:
The disciples ask when the rest of the dead will come and when the new world will begin. Jesus's answer is one of the clearest statements of realized eschatology in any tradition. What you look forward to has already come, but you do not recognize it. This is not a promise for later. It is a diagnosis of now. The kingdom, the new creation, the resurrection life, the age to come — it is already present, and the problem is your eyes.

This is exactly what the synoptic Jesus says in Luke 17:20-21 — the kingdom of God is not coming with observable signs; the kingdom of God is within you and among you. And in Thomas 113 — the Father's kingdom is spread out on the earth, and people do not see it. Later Christianity gradually pushed the kingdom into the future — heaven after death, second coming at the end of time, apocalyptic rescue. Paul's letters accelerated this shift. But the earliest Jesus material keeps insisting the opposite. It is here. Right now. What you are waiting for is already surrounding you. The failure is not one of timing but of recognition — the eye that has not yet learned to see the kingdom you are already standing in. *Metanoia* is the turning that makes the recognition possible.

jesus_words: His disciples said to him, "Twenty-four prophets spoke in Israel, and all of them spoke in you." He said to them, "You have omitted the one living in your presence and have spoken (only) of the dead."
title: The Living Among You
pullquote: Twenty-four prophets spoke of him. And they're still only talking about the dead one you're missing right now.
core_message: Reverence for past prophets is worthless if you cannot recognize the living presence right in front of you.
context:
The disciples try to compliment Jesus by placing him in the line of the twenty-four prophets of Israel — the traditional count of the Hebrew Bible's prophetic books. All of them spoke of you. Jesus is not flattered. You have omitted the one living in your presence and have spoken only of the dead. It is a sharp corrective. Do not bury me under a stack of ancestors. Notice me now.

This is a permanent temptation in religion. It is easier to venerate dead prophets than to listen to living ones. The Pharisees built tombs for the prophets their fathers had killed while missing the prophet standing in front of them (Mt 23:29-31; Lk 11:47-48). Two thousand years later, Christians study a two-thousand-year-old Jesus while ignoring the living Christ within — the same presence he told his followers is already among them, closer than breath. The Jesus Way is not archaeology. It is contact. The living one is available now, and the danger of any tradition is that reverence for the past can become an elaborate way of avoiding the present. Do not talk about the dead when the living is standing right here.

jesus_words: His disciples said to him, "Is circumcision beneficial or not?" He said to them, "If it were beneficial, their father would beget them already circumcised from their mother. Rather, the true circumcision in spirit has become completely profitable."
title: Circumcision in Spirit
pullquote: If circumcision mattered, babies would arrive that way. What matters is the circumcision of the heart.
core_message: External religious markers count for nothing; only the inward circumcision of the heart is real.
context:
The disciples ask a live question of the first century — is circumcision beneficial. Jesus's answer is deadpan and devastating. If it were beneficial, their father would beget them already circumcised from their mother. The argument from design cuts the ritual off at the knees. God did not include it in the equipment. Rather, the true circumcision in spirit has become completely profitable.

This is not new territory. The Hebrew Bible itself repeatedly relocates circumcision from the flesh to the heart. Deuteronomy 10:16 — circumcise the foreskin of your heart. Deuteronomy 30:6 — the Lord your God will circumcise your heart. Jeremiah 4:4 — circumcise yourselves to the Lord, remove the foreskin of your hearts. Jesus is standing squarely in that prophetic tradition. The external mark was never the point. The internal transformation always was. This becomes explosive in the first-century context because circumcision was the boundary marker of Jewish identity, the ritual that separated insider from outsider. Jesus, like the prophets before him, refuses to let the boundary be physical. What God wants is not a cut in the flesh but a change in the heart — the same *metanoia* running through everything he taught. The Jerusalem community around James eventually had to fight this out (Acts 15), and even then the argument continued. Thomas 53 preserves the original answer with no compromise.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Whoever has come to understand the world has found (only) a corpse, and whoever has found a corpse is superior to the world."
title: The World is a Corpse
pullquote: See the world for what it is and you are no longer owned by it. Understanding is the first act of freedom.
core_message: Once you truly understand the world of appearances, you see it is lifeless, and that seeing lifts you above it.
context:
This is a Thomas saying with the bite of Ecclesiastes. Once you look through the world of power, status, and possession, you find nothing living there — just a shell that outlives whoever chased it. Solomon called it *hevel* — vapor, breath. Thomas calls it a corpse. Same insight. The world people are scrambling to own is already dead; only the scramble keeps it looking alive. To understand this is to stop feeding the illusion.

The paradox is the second half. Whoever finds the corpse is superior to it. Seeing clearly is the whole liberation — no ritual, no priest, no sacrifice required. This lines up with Jesus's constant warning against storing up treasure on earth (Mt 6:19), against gaining the whole world and losing your *psyche* (Mk 8:36), and with his instruction to the rich young man to let it all go (Mk 10:21). The Nazarene and Ebionim communities lived from this understanding — voluntary poverty, shared goods, no allegiance to Rome or Temple. Thomas 56 is the philosophical spine of that way of life. Once the world is unmasked, its grip breaks. That is the beginning of the kingdom.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Blessed is the man who has suffered and found life."
title: Blessed is the One Who Has Suffered
pullquote: Suffering is not the point. What you find on the other side of it is.
core_message: Suffering that leads to real life is a blessing, because it burns away what was never you to begin with.
context:
This is a Thomas beatitude that never made it into Matthew's collection, but it belongs alongside them. Jesus is not glorifying pain — he is naming what suffering can do when it is received rather than resisted. It strips away the false self. It ends the illusion that the ego can control outcomes. When the constructed identity collapses under weight it cannot carry, what remains is the life that was underneath the whole time. That is why the saying blesses the one who *has* suffered — past tense — and found life. The finding is the point.

This maps onto everything Jesus said about losing your *psyche* to find it (Mt 10:39; Mk 8:35; Lk 17:33; Jn 12:25 — five attestations, one of the most repeated teachings in the record). It is also the pattern of the cross itself — not death for its own sake, but death of the ego-self as the doorway to real life. James, the brother of Jesus, put it the same way: consider it pure joy when you face trials, because the testing produces something (Jas 1:2-4). The Two Ways tradition (Deut 30; Didache 1; 1QS 3-4) assumes the same — the narrow road runs through hardship because that is where the false self runs out of road. Blessed is the one who kept walking.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Take heed of the living one while you are alive, lest you die and seek to see him and be unable to do so."
title: While You Are Alive
pullquote: You will not find after death what you refused to seek while living. The kingdom has a threshold, and it is here.
core_message: Seek the living presence of God now while you are able, because the search cannot be deferred to after you die.
context:
This is one of Thomas's most sober sayings. Jesus is not threatening hell. He is stating a fact about consciousness. The window for waking up is this life. Whatever capacity you build now for perceiving the living one — the presence of God within and around you — is the capacity you carry forward. Whatever you fail to cultivate is not automatically handed to you later. The search has to happen while there is still someone here to search.

This pairs directly with Jesus's core teaching that the kingdom is within you and around you right now (Lk 17:21; Thomas 3, 113). It is not a location you arrive at after death; it is a reality you learn to perceive while alive. The Lord's Prayer is present tense — *thy kingdom come*, on earth as in heaven. Deuteronomy 30 put it the same way: choose life *today*, so that you may live. The Two Ways tradition never speaks of the choice as postponable. Jesus is echoing that same urgency. Do not sleepwalk through the one life in which the door is standing open. Take heed. Look. The living one is here now — but only if you look now.

jesus_words: <They saw> a Samaritan carrying a lamb on his way to Judea. He said to his disciples, "That man is round about the lamb." They said to him, "So that he may kill it and eat it." He said to them, "While it is alive, he will not eat it, but only when he has killed it and it has become a corpse." They said to him, "He cannot do so otherwise." He said to them, "You too, look for a place for yourself within repose, lest you become a corpse and be eaten."
title: Do Not Become a Corpse
pullquote: Whatever you feed on, you become. Find your rest in the living, or you will be eaten by what you served.
core_message: Live in an inner state of repose grounded in the living God, or you become spiritually dead and consumed by the world.
context:
The disciples watch a Samaritan carry a lamb toward Judea, and they know the lamb will end up on a plate. Jesus turns it into a mirror. The lamb has to die to be eaten — and Jesus is telling his followers not to die that same death. Do not become a corpse. Do not let yourself go so cold, so cut off from the living center, that the world can swallow you whole. Find your place within *repose* — the still, alive presence of God — while there is still time to find it.

The saying works on two layers. There is a plain reading — a nod, perhaps, to the sacrificial economy the Nazarene community rejected. The Gospel of the Ebionites (preserved by Epiphanius, *Panarion* 30.16.5) has Jesus saying *I have come to abolish the sacrifices*, and Hosea 6:6 stands behind everything he taught about mercy over slaughter. The lamb on its way to Judea evokes the whole Temple machine. But the deeper layer is inward. Whatever you rest in becomes what you are. Rest in fear, in grievance, in ambition, in the world's noise — and those things eat you from the inside until nothing living is left. Rest in the living one and you cannot be consumed. Jesus is inviting his students into the same interior stillness he lived from himself.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "If one who knows the all still feels a personal deficiency, he is completely deficient."
title: Knowing the All
pullquote: If you have touched the fullness of God and still feel empty, you have not touched it at all.
core_message: Anyone who claims to know the whole and still feels lacking has not actually known it.
context:
This saying is a diagnostic. Jesus is not shaming the deficient — he is describing what real awakening produces. When you have actually perceived the fullness of God (the *pleroma*, the all, what Paul in a rare moment of clarity called the fullness in whom you are complete), you cannot simultaneously feel a personal lack. The two states are mutually exclusive. So if the sense of deficiency is still driving you — needing to be seen, needing more, needing to be right — the knowing has not landed. It is still theoretical.

This lines up with Jesus's teaching on the kingdom as an inner reality (Lk 17:21; Thomas 3, 113). It also echoes Psalm 23 — the Lord is my shepherd, *I shall not want*. Contentment is the marker. It is not a mood you talk yourself into; it is the natural residue of actually perceiving that everything is already held in God. Paul, on a good day, said the same thing (Phil 4:11-13). The Nazarene and Ebionim communities lived from this assumption — no possessions, no anxiety about tomorrow, all needs met from the common purse and from providence. If you know the all and still feel the ache of not enough, keep going. Something has not yet arrived.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "That which you have will save you if you bring it forth from yourselves. That which you do not have within you will kill you if you do not have it within you."
title: Bring It Forth
pullquote: The kingdom is not something you download from outside. It is something you deliver from inside — or it kills you.
core_message: What lives within you must be brought out to save you, and what is not there cannot save you at all.
context:
This is one of Thomas's sharpest lines. There is no external rescue. Whatever will save you has to already be in you — and it has to be brought forth, expressed, lived, given away. Hidden, it does nothing. Undeveloped, it does nothing. The parable of the talents makes the same point (Mt 25:14-30) — the servant who buried his gift is the one who lost everything. The kingdom does not arrive from the sky. It rises from the inside and out into the world through your life. That is the whole shape of Jesus's way.

And the second half is the warning. What you do not have inside you will kill you if you do not have it inside you. Not a threat — a physics. If forgiveness is not in you, unforgiveness will corrode you. If love is not in you, fear will eat you. If trust — *pistis* — is not in you, anxiety will run the whole show. This is the same principle as reciprocity (Lk 6:37-38): what you give is what you get, and what is not in you cannot flow through you. The kingdom is within you (Lk 17:21). Bring it out. Everything Jesus taught in the Sermon on the Mount was a manual for doing exactly that.

jesus_words: He said, "O Lord, there are many around the drinking trough, but there is nothing in the cistern."
title: Nothing in the Cistern
pullquote: A crowd around the trough. A dry well underneath. Presence without depth is the perennial danger.
core_message: Many gather around the source, but the source itself has run dry when there is nothing living underneath.
context:
This little saying reads like a lament, spoken to the Lord by someone in the community — perhaps a disciple, perhaps Jesus himself. Many are drawn to the outward form of the teaching. Few have done the interior work that fills the cistern in the first place. Crowds around a trough with no water underneath is a picture of religion without transformation. It is a picture of Jesus's own following at points in his ministry — thousands gathered for bread and healing, hundreds by the end, eleven at the cross.

The imagery is drawn straight from Jeremiah. God's complaint through the prophet was that his people had done two evils — they had forsaken him, the *fountain of living waters*, and hewn out for themselves cisterns, *broken cisterns that can hold no water* (Jer 2:13). Thomas 74 is that same complaint compressed into one line. The Nazarene community centered its life on living water — flowing, immersive, un-stored — over against the still, stagnant water of the Temple mikvaot. Jesus uses the same language with the Samaritan woman (Jn 4:10-14) and in the Temple itself (Jn 7:38). The teaching is unchanged. Do not gather around a dry cistern and call it faith. Go to the source that flows.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "He who has recognized the world has found the body, but he who has found the body is superior to the world."
title: Found the Body
pullquote: Understand the world and you find only a body. Find the body and you already stand above it.
core_message: Recognizing the world for what it materially is puts you above being ruled by it.
context:
Thomas 80 is a near-twin of Thomas 56 — the same insight in slightly different key. Where 56 says *corpse*, 80 says *body*. Both are contrasting the world of matter and appearance with the awareness that perceives it. When you have actually recognized the world — its impermanence, its emptiness of the deep life you were looking for — you have found the body. And whoever has found the body is superior to it. Perception itself is the liberation.

This is not world-hating. Jesus was not a Gnostic in the later sense — he blessed bread, healed bodies, ate with sinners, celebrated weddings. The point is not that matter is evil. The point is that matter is not where the living one lives. Confusing the surface for the source is the whole problem. The kingdom is within (Lk 17:21). Life is with the Father. The world is real, but it is a body, not the soul. When you see the world for what it is, you stop asking the world to give you what only God can give. That is the freedom. Storing up treasure in heaven (Mt 6:19-21) is not about the afterlife — it is about where you locate your center of gravity right now.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Let him who has grown rich be king, and let him who possesses power renounce it."
title: Renounce Power
pullquote: If you have grown rich, take the throne. If you have taken the throne, put it down. Kingdom logic runs upside-down.
core_message: Real spiritual authority comes to those who let go of the power the world hands them.
context:
This is Thomas turning the world's operating system on its head. Let the rich one become king — sure, take the crown you have been chasing. But whoever actually holds power, renounce it. The saying is not endorsing wealth and rule. It is exposing them. If you climb the ladder all the way to the top, the only sane thing to do at the summit is to step off. The path of the world ends in a renunciation, or it ends in ruin. There is no third option.

This is the same pattern as Jesus's teaching that the greatest among you must be the servant of all (Mk 10:42-45; Mt 20:25-28; Lk 22:25-27 — three attestations, plus John's foot-washing in Jn 13). It is the pattern of the rich young man who could not let go (Mk 10:17-22). It is the shape of Jesus's own life — refusing the wilderness temptation to rule the kingdoms of the world (Mt 4:8-10). The Ebionim — *the poor ones* — were living this deliberately, selling possessions and pooling everything (Acts 2:44-45; 4:32-35; 1QS 6). Power ungiven becomes a prison. Power given away becomes the kingdom. Jesus modelled it to the end.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "The images are manifest to man, but the light in them remains concealed in the image of the light of the father. He will become manifest, but his image will remain concealed by his light."
title: The Light in the Image
pullquote: Everything visible is carrying a hidden light. The Father shows himself and hides himself in the same act.
core_message: The visible forms of the world contain a concealed divine light that reveals God even while veiling him.
context:
This is Thomas at its most contemplative. Images — every visible form, every face, every leaf — are manifest to us. But the light inside them, the light of the Father that gives them being, stays concealed inside the image. And when that light does become manifest, the image itself becomes the veil. God shows and hides in a single motion. This is how the presence works. You cannot look directly at the sun; you see it in what it lights up. You cannot look directly at God; you see God in what God is making right now.

This is the same theology as Psalm 19 — the heavens declare the glory of God, and no speech is used. It is the same as Romans 1:20 — the invisible things are seen through the things that are made. Jesus taught the same in his own way: consider the lilies (Mt 6:28); the kingdom is like a mustard seed, like leaven, like a treasure hidden in a field (Mt 13). The Father is not far away hiding behind the world. The Father is present in it and through it — visible if you have the eyes for it, invisible if you do not. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Mt 5:8). The seeing is a capacity, not a location.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "When you see your likeness, you rejoice. But when you see your images which came into being before you, and which neither die not become manifest, how much you will have to bear!"
title: The Images That Came Before You
pullquote: You rejoice at your reflection. Wait until you see the self that was before the reflection began.
core_message: The transient likeness you love is easy; the eternal image behind it will be harder to bear.
context:
You look in the mirror and enjoy what you see — the face, the personality, the story of yourself you have curated. That likeness is comfortable. Jesus is pointing to something else. There is an image of you that came into being before you did — the eternal blueprint, the *imago Dei*, what Genesis 1:27 calls the image and likeness of God. That image does not die and does not become manifest in the ordinary way. To meet it is to meet what you actually are underneath the personality. And it will cost you.

Meeting your true self is what Jesus meant by finding your *psyche* by losing it (Mt 10:39; Mk 8:35). The constructed identity has to go for the real one to be seen. That is why he said *how much you will have to bear* — the process is hard. The Nazarene practices of immersion, silence, poverty, and community existed to strip the false self back to the eternal one. Thomas 84 is describing the same journey the Sermon on the Mount describes from a different angle. The good news is that the image is already there. You did not have to create it. You only have to stop hiding from it.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Adam came into being from a great power and a great wealth, but he did not become worthy of you. For had he been worthy, he would not have experienced death."
title: Adam Was Not Worthy
pullquote: The first human had every advantage and still fell. You have something Adam did not — and you are meant to surpass him.
core_message: Adam had great power and wealth but was not worthy of the awakening now offered to Jesus's disciples.
context:
This is a hard saying to hear at first. Adam — the archetype of humanity — came into being with every advantage. Great power. Great wealth. Made in the image, walking with God in the garden. And still he did not become worthy of what Jesus is offering his disciples. If he had been worthy, he would not have experienced death. The saying is not condemning Adam personally. It is naming the whole condition Jesus came to answer. The first human fell asleep. The second human — the *bar enasha*, the human one — came to wake everyone up.

This is why Paul, at least here, was tracking with something Jesus said: the first Adam became a living being, the last Adam a life-giving spirit (1 Cor 15:45). Jesus is not offering a return to Eden. He is offering something Adam never had — full, conscious participation in the Father, on this side of the fall. The Nazarene apocalyptic worldview held that a new humanity was arriving, and this saying assumes it. You are meant to surpass Adam. That is the invitation. Not through effort, not through law-keeping, but through the awakening (*metanoia*) Jesus is holding out. What Adam lost by unconsciousness, you are meant to inherit by consciousness.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Wretched is the body that is dependant upon a body, and wretched is the soul that is dependent on these two."
title: Body Depending on Body
pullquote: When flesh clings to flesh and soul clings to both, everything is upside-down. Rest in what does not decay.
core_message: A life whose body depends on other bodies and whose soul depends on those bodies is a life in bondage.
context:
The saying is stacked. A body that depends on another body — needing another person to complete it, to define it, to prop it up — is already in trouble. A soul that depends on those two dependent bodies is in even worse trouble. Jesus is describing the whole chain of misplaced dependency that runs modern life: needing the other person, needing their approval, and staking your inner state on that dependency. Wretched. Not because bodies are evil, but because bodies cannot bear the weight of being your source.

This is the same teaching as the Sermon on the Mount's instruction to seek first the kingdom (Mt 6:33). The Father is the source. When you are grounded in that reality, other relationships become gifts rather than lifelines. When you are ungrounded, they become the lifeline you drown clinging to. The Nazarene community structured itself around this — no clinging to family that owned you (Lk 14:26), no clinging to possessions (Mk 10:21), no clinging to status. Not because relationships and things are bad, but because a soul propped up by them cannot rest. Rest belongs to whoever is grounded in the living one (Thomas 60). Wretched is what happens when the whole tower is built on borrowed foundations.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "The angels and the prophets will come to you and give to you those things you (already) have. And you too, give them those things which you have, and say to yourselves, 'When will they come and take what is theirs?'"
title: Give What You Have
pullquote: The angels and prophets bring you what is already yours. Pass it on and ask when what belongs to them will be claimed.
core_message: Give away what you already possess spiritually, and expect that what is yours to receive will find you.
context:
This is an odd, luminous saying. Angels and prophets come and give you things you already have — the truth was in you before they arrived; they only reflect it back and confirm it. That is the whole function of a genuine teacher, and it is what Jesus said about himself elsewhere: the kingdom is within you (Lk 17:21). The teacher does not implant the kingdom. The teacher points you to what is already there. So when the angels and prophets deliver, they are giving you your own.

And then the turn: you too, give what you have. And ask yourselves — when will they come and take what is theirs? Meaning, when will the deep receiving happen that answers the giving? The saying reads like a picture of reciprocity in the spiritual economy. Give and it will be given (Lk 6:38). Freely you have received, freely give (Mt 10:8). What you send out returns, and what is yours to receive is waiting on your capacity to make room. This is the same operating system as the Golden Rule, applied to inner life. The measure you give is the measure you get. Angels and prophets included.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "The kingdom of the father is like a certain woman who was carrying a jar full of meal. While she was walking on the road, still some distance from home, the handle of the jar broke and the meal emptied out behind her on the road. She did not realize it; she had noticed no accident. When she reached her house, she set the jar down and found it empty."
title: The Empty Jar
pullquote: The kingdom does not always slip away with a bang. Sometimes it just leaks out behind you while you walk.
core_message: The kingdom can be lost quietly through inattention, without any dramatic failure, until you arrive home and find nothing left.
context:
This is one of Thomas's most disturbing parables, and it belongs beside Jesus's other warnings about inattention. A woman walks home from the mill with a jar of meal. The handle breaks. Meal trickles out behind her the whole way home. She notices nothing. She sets the jar down. It is empty. That is the whole story. No enemy stole from her. No storm broke the jar. Her own inattention did the work. When she finally looked, everything was gone.

The kingdom is like this. Not always dramatic loss — often just a slow leak, one distracted day at a time, one small compromise, one unnoticed drift, until the interior life you thought you had is not there anymore. Jesus warned the same thing in different keys: watch and pray, stay awake, keep your lamp trimmed (Mt 25:1-13; Mk 13:33-37; Lk 12:35-40 — multiple attestations). The Two Ways is not a one-time choice. It is a daily walk on which attention is the whole practice. Paul's confess-and-you're-saved formula (Rom 10:9) has no answer to this parable, because the leak keeps happening whether you have said the words or not. Only *staying awake* keeps the jar full.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "The kingdom of the father is like a certain man who wanted to kill a powerful man. In his own house he drew his sword and stuck it into the wall in order to find out whether his hand could carry through. Then he slew the powerful man."
title: Testing the Sword
pullquote: Practice at home what you intend to do in the world. The kingdom is built the same way.
core_message: The kingdom is like someone who first tests his capacity privately before acting on it publicly.
context:
This is one of the strangest kingdom parables in any gospel, and it does not appear in the canon. A man wants to kill a powerful man. Before he tries, he stabs his sword into his own wall to see whether his hand can carry the blow through. It can. So he goes and does the deed. The violent frame is startling — but the kingdom principle underneath is one Jesus taught in gentler forms. Count the cost before you build the tower. Do not go to war without first sitting down to see if you can win (Lk 14:28-32).

What you intend to do in the world, practice at home first. What you cannot yet do interiorly, you will not be able to do exteriorly. The person who wants to love enemies has to test the sword — first in prayer, in small provocations, in the household — before facing the real adversary. The kingdom is not built by sudden bursts of heroism; it is built by tested capacity. The Nazarene community's whole formation process assumed this — years of discipline before responsibility (1QS 6-7 lays out the same pattern). Jesus wants disciples who have already made the interior stroke. When the moment comes in the world, the arm is ready.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Woe to the pharisees, for they are like a dog sleeping in the manger of oxen, for neither does he eat nor does he let the oxen eat."
title: Dog in the Manger
pullquote: They will not enter, and they will not let anyone else in either. That is the whole indictment.
core_message: The Pharisees block others from what they themselves refuse to receive.
context:
This saying has close cousins in the canonical woes. Woe to you experts in the law, Jesus says in Luke 11:52, because you have taken away the key to knowledge — you did not enter yourselves, and you hindered those who were entering. Matthew 23:13 says the same: you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces; you neither enter yourselves nor let those enter who are trying to. Thomas 102 gives the picture in one homely image. A dog lies in the manger of the oxen. He is not going to eat the hay. He will not let the oxen eat it either. Pure obstruction with no benefit to anyone, including himself.

This is a searing description of religion that guards a door it will not walk through. The Pharisees knew the tradition better than anyone. They studied it, argued it, defended it. But they did not enter the reality it pointed to — the mercy, the love, the kingdom within. And their gatekeeping stopped others too. Jesus reserved his sharpest anger for this pattern (Mt 23 as a whole; Mk 7:6-13 on tradition versus the commandment). The 613 laws of the scribes — what Jeremiah 8:8 called *the lying pen of the scribes* — became the manger the dog lay in. The way Jesus taught was the exact opposite: an open door, low bar, kingdom already available. If you are not going to enter, at least get out of the way.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "He who knows the father and the mother will be called the son of a harlot."
title: Son of a Harlot
pullquote: Know your true origin, and the world will insult you for it. The insult is the mark of the awakening.
core_message: Whoever knows the true source of their being will be slandered by a world that only recognizes worldly parentage.
context:
This is one of Thomas's cryptic sayings, and it takes some unfolding. In first-century Palestine, calling someone the *son of a harlot* was the gravest insult — an attack on legitimacy, honor, family name, standing in the community. Jesus says: whoever knows the true father and mother — the divine origin, the source beyond biological parentage — will get called exactly that. Because to know your true origin is to sit lightly to your worldly one, and a world that only understands worldly lineage cannot help but slander you for it.

The undertone is autobiographical. Jesus himself was called precisely that by his opponents (Jn 8:41 — *we are not born of fornication*, an insinuation cast his way). His teaching that his true family were those who did the will of the Father (Mk 3:31-35; Mt 12:46-50; Lk 8:19-21) reframed lineage entirely. To *know the father and the mother* in Thomas's sense is to know God as the source and creation as the mother — a Nazarene understanding echoed elsewhere in Thomas (Thomas 101, 105). Anyone who lives from that knowing will be misread by the world. That misreading — being called what you are not — is one of the marks of walking the narrow road. Blessed are you when they insult you falsely for my sake (Mt 5:11).

jesus_words: Jesus said, "He who will drink from my mouth will become like me. I myself shall become he, and the things that are hidden will be revealed to him."
title: Drink From My Mouth
pullquote: The teacher and the student become one. That is the whole point of a rabbi and a talmid.
core_message: Whoever fully receives Jesus's teaching becomes like him and receives revelation of what is hidden.
context:
This is the *talmid* relationship spelled out in one line. In the first-century rabbinic world, a disciple did not just learn the rabbi's ideas — the disciple *became* the rabbi. Same walk, same speech, same responses to trouble. Jesus said it plainly in Matthew 10:24-25 and Luke 6:40: it is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher. John 13:15 — I have given you an example. Thomas 108 says the same thing in more intimate language. Whoever drinks from my mouth — receives the teaching directly, without filter, without dilution — becomes like me. And *I myself shall become he*. The two collapse into one shared reality.

This is the whole New Testament vision of Christ, reduced to a single mystical sentence. Not worship the teacher from a safe distance. Become the teacher. Live the way he lived. That was Jesus's whole plan — to reproduce the Christ-life in his disciples so the kingdom would keep going after him (Jn 14:12 — greater works than these). Deification came in 325 at Nicaea and turned the invitation into an object of adoration; the earlier Jewish-Christian understanding — preserved in Thomas, in the Hebrew Gospel, and in the Ebionim tradition — kept the emphasis where Jesus put it. Drink from the mouth. Become like the teacher. Then what was hidden becomes revealed — because you are now looking from inside.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Whoever finds the world and becomes rich, let him renounce the world."
title: Renounce the World
pullquote: If you have found the world and grown rich in it, the next move is to let it go. Otherwise it owns you.
core_message: Whoever succeeds in the world's terms must then renounce the world to stay free.
context:
This is Thomas 81 in slightly different wording, and it points to the same reality. You can succeed on the world's terms — accumulate, achieve, get everything you were told to want. And once you have, the only sane response is to let it go. Not because the world is evil, but because possession without renunciation reverses the ownership. What you clutch begins to clutch you. Jesus watched a rich young man discover this in real time (Mk 10:17-22). He had kept the commandments. He had done well. The one thing he lacked was the freedom to let go. And he walked away grieved.

The Nazarene / Ebionim community made this the entry requirement. Sell what you have. Give to the poor. Follow (Mk 10:21; Acts 2:44-45; 4:32-35; 1QS 6). The community's very name — Ebionim, *the poor ones* — announced what they had renounced and what they had chosen instead. This is not asceticism for its own sake. It is the practical requirement of a heart that can actually love God and neighbor without divided loyalties. You cannot serve God and *mammon* (Mt 6:24). If you have grown rich, renounce. The renouncing is the doorway.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "The heavens and the earth will be rolled up in your presence. And the one who lives from the living one will not see death." Does not Jesus say, "Whoever finds himself is superior to the world?"
title: Whoever Finds Himself
pullquote: Heaven and earth roll up in your presence when you know who you are. Find the self, transcend the world.
core_message: Whoever lives from the living source and finds their true self is beyond death and above the world.
context:
This saying is two teachings stitched together. First — the heavens and the earth will be rolled up in your presence. Not a cosmic destruction from outside, but a shift in what you see. When you awaken, the whole system of appearances loses the ultimacy it seemed to have. It rolls up like a scroll (echoing Isaiah 34:4 and used again in Revelation 6:14 — but here re-cast interiorly). The one who lives from the living one will not see death. This is Jesus's core promise, in many keys — whoever keeps my word will never taste death (Jn 8:51-52); everyone living and believing in me shall never die (Jn 11:26); the kingdom is within (Lk 17:21).

And then Thomas 111 turns and asks the disciples to answer their own question. *Does not Jesus say, whoever finds himself is superior to the world?* Finding yourself — the true self, the eternal image (Thomas 84), not the constructed personality — is the whole liberation. From that vantage the world no longer looms. It rolls up. The Nazarene apocalyptic hope of a new heaven and new earth got translated by Jesus into an interior event that begins here and now. The end of the world is already happening in every awakened heart.

jesus_words: Jesus said, "Woe to the flesh that depends on the soul; woe to the soul that depends on the flesh."
title: Flesh and Soul
pullquote: Neither is meant to lean on the other. Both were meant to lean on God.
core_message: A flesh that leans on soul and a soul that leans on flesh are both in trouble — both were made to rest in God.
context:
This paired *woe* is deceptively simple. Woe to the flesh that depends on the soul. Woe to the soul that depends on the flesh. Neither dependency works. If your body-life is trying to draw its meaning from your interior life, and your interior life is trying to draw its meaning from your body-life, the whole system collapses into itself. Both flesh and soul were made to rest in the Father — the *living one* Thomas keeps naming. Any other arrangement is bondage.

This is not the Greek dualism that later Christianity absorbed, where flesh is bad and spirit is good. Jesus was Jewish. He blessed bread and fish, he touched lepers, he wept at graves. Body and soul are both good. What he is warning against is the wrong hierarchy — either using the interior to prop up the exterior (spiritualizing to justify appetite) or using the exterior to prop up the interior (looking to appearances to give you an identity). Both are backwards. The right order is what Jesus prayed: our Father, thy will, thy kingdom, on earth as in heaven (Mt 6:9-10). Body and soul both aligned upward, both grounded in the source. That is the way the whole life stops being wretched and starts being kingdom.

jesus_words: Simon Peter said to him, "Let Mary leave us, for women are not worthy of life." Jesus said, "I myself shall lead her in order to make her male, so that she too may become a living spirit resembling you males. For every woman who will make herself male will enter the kingdom of heaven." The Gospel According to Thomas
title: Mary Made Living Spirit
pullquote: Peter tries to exclude Mary. Jesus refuses. Whoever awakens the living spirit — man or woman — is in the kingdom.
core_message: Jesus defends Mary against Peter's exclusion and declares that every woman who awakens the living spirit within enters the kingdom.
context:
This is the most controversial saying in Thomas, and the most misread. Peter says let Mary leave us, for women are not worthy of life — a straight statement of the patriarchal assumption of the era. Jesus refuses. He says he himself will lead her, so that she too becomes a *living spirit* like the male disciples. In first-century language, *male* was code for the fully-realized human — active, awake, participating. *Female*, in this same rhetorical frame, meant the un-awakened, the receptive-only, the not-yet. Jesus is not erasing Mary. He is dignifying her. He is telling Peter that she has the same access to becoming a living spirit that any of them do. The saying is Jesus's refusal to let his community exclude women — a refusal consistent with everything the gospels report about him.

Jesus consistently included women in ways scandalous to his culture. Mary Magdalene funded his ministry (Lk 8:1-3). The Samaritan woman became the first evangelist (Jn 4). Mary of Bethany sat at his feet as a disciple (Lk 10:38-42). Women were the first witnesses to the resurrection (Mk 16; Mt 28; Lk 24; Jn 20). The Gospel of Mary shows her teaching the male disciples what the Savior told her. Thomas 114 is the earliest scene of the tension between Peter and Mary that runs through several of the extra-canonical gospels — and Jesus, in every version, sides with Mary. The saying that sounds sexist on modern ears is in fact Jesus dismantling Peter's sexism by insisting Mary belongs.

jesus_words: "Every nature, every form, every creature exists in and with each other, but they'll dissolve again into their own roots, because the nature of matter dissolves into its nature alone. Anyone who has ears to hear should hear! ... Sin doesn't exist, but you're the ones who make sin when you act in accordance with the nature of adultery, which is called 'sin.' That's why the Good came among you, up to the things of every nature in order to restore it within its root. ... That's why you get sick and die, because you love what tricks you. Anyone who can understand should understand! Matter gave birth to a passion that has no image because it came from what's contrary to nature. Then confusion arises in the whole body. That's why I told you to be content at heart. If you're discontented, find contentment in the presence of the various images of nature."
title: What Matter Cannot Hold
pullquote: Sin does not exist as a thing. It is what you make when you act against your true nature.
core_message: Every created form returns to its root, sin is not a substance but an action against nature, and inner contentment is the medicine.
context:
This is a rich teaching from the Savior in the Gospel of Mary — dialogue material recorded in the community around Mary Magdalene after the resurrection. The Savior begins with metaphysics. Every nature, every form, every creature holds together in mutual dependence and eventually dissolves back into its own root. Matter returns to matter. Nothing here is being demonized — this is simply how the material order works. Then the pivot that jumps off the page: *sin does not exist*. Not as a substance, not as a stain, not as a thing baked into you at birth. Sin is what you *make* when you act contrary to your true nature. It is a verb, not a noun. This is exactly the Jesus Way understanding of sin — harm you do, not a metaphysical debt you owe.

The Good — the Christ presence — came among people to restore every nature back into its root, back into alignment with what it was made to be. Sickness and death arise, the Savior says, from loving what tricks you — attachment to what cannot hold you. The prescription is to *be content at heart*. That is the same instruction Paul got in a lucid moment (Phil 4:11) and the same instruction the Psalms return to (Ps 23, Ps 131). Contentment is not passivity. It is the interior state that has stopped chasing what matter cannot deliver. This teaching contradicts the entire later doctrine of original sin as an inherited stain requiring blood atonement. There is no such stain here. There is only the ongoing invitation to return to root and rest.
notes: Gospel of Mary interlinear (Berlin Codex BG 8502,1)

jesus_words: "Peace be with you! Acquire my peace. Be careful not to let anyone mislead you by saying, 'Look over here!' or 'Look over there!' Because the Son of Humanity exists within you. Follow him! Those who seek him will find him. Go then and preach the gospel about the kingdom. Don't lay down any rules beyond what I've given you, nor make a law like the lawgiver, lest you be bound by it."
title: Peace Be With You
pullquote: The Son of Humanity is within you. Follow him. And do not build a new law where he refused to build one.
core_message: Jesus commissions the disciples with peace, tells them the kingdom is within, and forbids adding rules or laws beyond what he taught.
context:
This is the Savior's parting instruction in the Gospel of Mary, and it is one of the most concentrated summaries of the Jesus Way anywhere in the early literature. Peace be with you. Acquire my peace — meaning it is a state to be cultivated, not just a greeting. Then the warning against being misled by anyone pointing outward — do not look over here, do not look over there. Why? Because *the Son of Humanity exists within you*. This is the *bar enasha*, the human one, present as an interior reality. It is Luke 17:21 in different wording, and Thomas 3, and Thomas 113. The whole gospel of Jesus in one line — the kingdom, the Christ, the son of the human, is within.

Then the commission. Go preach the gospel about the kingdom — the good news that the kingdom is here, now, within and among people. And then the extraordinary command: *do not lay down any rules beyond what I've given you, nor make a law like the lawgiver, lest you be bound by it.* This is Jesus telling his disciples not to become new Moses figures generating new legal codes. The law he gave was already reduced to its essence — love God, love neighbor (Mk 12:29-31). Do not add to it. The tragedy of church history is that this instruction was largely ignored — Paul built new theology, later councils built creeds and canons, and Christianity accumulated exactly the kind of legal apparatus the Savior warned against. Peace comes from the interior source. Rules built on top of it are the very trap he came to open.
notes: Gospel of Mary interlinear (Berlin Codex BG 8502,1)

jesus_words: "You're blessed because you didn't waver at the sight of me. For where the mind is, there is the treasure." (To Mary's vision query:) "They don't see in the soul or in the spirit, but the mind which exists between the two is what sees the vision."
title: Where the Mind Is
pullquote: The mind is what sees. Not the eyes, not the flesh — the faculty between soul and spirit that turns toward the treasure and beholds it.
core_message: You see spiritual reality with the mind that stands between soul and spirit, and where that mind is fixed, there your treasure lies.
context:
Mary Magdalene has just told the disciples that the risen teacher appeared to her in a vision. Peter and Andrew scoff. But in the fragment that survives, Jesus first blesses Mary for not wavering at the sight of him and gives the reason: where the mind is, there is the treasure. It is the same principle Jesus states in the Sermon on the Mount — where your treasure is, there your heart will be — turned around and sharpened. What you fix your mind on is what you have. Attention is possession. If your mind is fixed on the kingdom, you are in the kingdom. If it is fixed on lack, grievance, or fear, that is your treasure and that is where you live.

Then the anatomy of vision. The disciples ask how anyone actually sees the Lord in a vision — with soul or with spirit? Jesus answers that it is neither. It is the *nous* — the mind that stands between soul and spirit — that beholds. This is the same *nous* that undergoes *metanoia* — transformation of consciousness. It is not the reasoning intellect and it is not raw emotion. It is the inner faculty that can turn and see. The Gospel of Mary, preserved only in a fifth-century Coptic codex with pages missing, sits inside the same stream as Thomas 3 and Luke 17:21: the kingdom is inward, and it is seen by an inward organ. Mary is not making up a private mysticism — she is reporting what the teacher taught, and she is being told, plainly, that she got it right and the men who mocked her did not.
notes: Gospel of Mary interlinear (Berlin Codex BG 8502,1)

jesus_words: "My power, O power, thou hast forsaken me!"
title: My Power, My Power
pullquote: The Gospel of Peter's cry from the cross — not "my God" but "my power" — the divine strength within, spoken of as departing at the moment of death.
core_message: In the Gospel of Peter's cross scene, Jesus calls out to the divine power within him as it withdraws at the moment of death.
context:
The Gospel of Peter is a second-century passion narrative, known only in a fragment found at Akhmim in Egypt in 1886, and quoted by Bishop Serapion around 190 AD before he pulled it from his church for its unorthodox flavor. In its crucifixion scene, the cry from the cross is not the Psalm 22 line the canonical gospels give — *Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani* — but a different sentence: my power, O power, thou hast forsaken me. Then, the text says, he was taken up. The wording matters. Peter is not reporting the Aramaic of Psalm 22. He is describing an inward event — the *dynamis*, the divine power that had rested on Jesus through his ministry, departing at the moment of death.

Early Jewish-Christian groups read this line without embarrassment. For the Ebionim and the Nazarenes, Jesus was the human one — *bar enasha* — anointed and empowered by the Spirit from his baptism forward, the prophet-like-Moses of Deuteronomy 18. The power was real and it was God's, but it rested on a human being. What Peter's fragment preserves is that older way of speaking, before Nicaea in 325 AD collapsed the distinction and made Jesus co-eternal deity. It is the same instinct that shows up when Jesus turns healing back on the person — *your* faith has made you whole — and when he tells the disciples they will do greater works than these. The power is available. It rested on him, and the invitation of the Jesus way is that it can rest on you.

jesus_words: I am come to do away with sacrifices, and if you cease not sacrificing, the wrath of God will not cease from you.
title: I Come to Abolish Sacrifices
pullquote: "I am come to do away with sacrifices."
core_message: Jesus came to end the sacrificial system, not to complete it with his own blood.
context:
This is the sentence the Jesus Way keeps returning to, preserved outside the canon by the Ebionim — the poor ones, the community that traced its lineage through James the brother of Jesus and never left Jerusalem. Epiphanius quotes it in the 370s while attacking them, which is exactly why it survived: he needed to prove they were heretics for saying it. *I have come to do away with sacrifices, and if you cease not sacrificing, the wrath of God will not cease from you.* No sacrificial theology. No blood atonement. No lamb required. The Temple's whole economy — priest, altar, animal, blood, receipt — is what Jesus came to end. And the community closest to him in blood and geography preserved that teaching against every incentive to soften it.

The saying is not an outlier — it is the Nazarene position, spoken plainly. The Hebrew prophets Jesus quoted had said it first: God takes no delight in sacrifice (Ps 40:6, Ps 51:16), never asked for it (Jer 7:22), desires mercy and not sacrifice (Hos 6:6 — which Jesus quotes twice, Mt 9:13 and 12:7). Amos 5, Isaiah 1, Micah 6, Ps 40 all carry the same message. When Jesus cleansed the Temple with Jeremiah 7:11 on his lips, he was enacting this teaching, not improvising. And when Paul later built a theology on Jesus's blood as the required sacrifice (Rom 3:25, Heb 9:22), he wrote the opposite of what the Ebionim, closest to the source, said Jesus actually taught. Epiphanius accused the Ebionites of perverting Jesus's words only a hundred years after his death; the more likely reading is that they kept them, and the church that persecuted them changed them.
parallels_refs: Gospel of the Ebionites Panarion 30.16.4-5 | Hos 6:6; Jer 7:22; Ps 40:6; Ps 51:16; Amos 5:21-24; Micah 6:6-8; Isa 1:11-17 | Related: Mt 9:13; Mt 12:7 (Jesus citing Hos 6:6)
